steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise overview of the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks a hydroxyl (–OH) group at its 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has an –OH at the 2′ carbon. That extra hydroxyl makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine. Uracil pairs with adenine during base-pairing.

3. Strandedness and structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous right-handed double helix. Two complementary strands run antiparallel and are held together by hydrogen bonds.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded. It can fold back on itself via intramolecular base-pairing to form hairpins, bulges and more complex 3D shapes.

4. Location and function in cells  
   • DNA resides primarily in the cell nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes), with small amounts in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Its main role is long-term storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) or cytoplasm (prokaryotes) and then travels to various cellular compartments. It plays multiple roles:  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA) carries coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes.  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are central to protein synthesis.  
     – Regulatory RNAs (microRNA, siRNA, long noncoding RNA) control gene expression.  
     – Some RNA molecules (ribozymes) have catalytic activity.

5. Stability and lifespan  
   • DNA’s deoxyribose backbone and double-helix protect it from hydrolysis and enzymes, making it highly stable—ideal for archival storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA’s extra 2′-OH group makes it more prone to hydrolysis, and single strands are more accessible to nucleases. Cellular RNAs often have short half-lives, reflecting their transient regulatory and functional roles.

6. Replication and synthesis  
   • DNA is replicated by DNA polymerases prior to cell division, using each strand as a template.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA by RNA polymerases. In eukaryotes, mRNA is processed—capped, spliced and polyadenylated—before export to the cytoplasm.

7. Viral genomes  
   • Some viruses store their genomes as DNA (e.g., herpesviruses), while others use RNA—either single-stranded (e.g., influenza, HIV) or double-stranded (e.g., rotavirus).

Summary  
DNA is the chemically stable, double-stranded blueprint of life, using deoxyribose and thymine to store long-term genetic information. RNA is the more versatile, usually single-stranded cousin that uses ribose and uracil to carry genetic messages, catalyze reactions and regulate genes—but at the cost of lower chemical stability.
